tagline.text: Leyte's gateway, risen again with the Santo Niño, MacArthur and the memory of Haiyan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–June (relatively clear), Santo Niño fiesta in late June

children.text: The largest city in Eastern Visayas sits on Leyte Gulf and gathers in one place the Santo Niño Church, the shrine museum built by Imelda Marcos, the mansion that served as MacArthur's headquarters, and a shipwreck memorial left by Haiyan's storm surge. It is also the gateway where trips through Leyte and Samar begin and end.

Tacloban is the main city of Eastern Visayas, set at the northeastern tip of Leyte Island where the San Juanico Strait opens into Leyte Gulf. It is the capital of Leyte Province and the economic and transport hub of the region, home to about 260,000 people according to the
census. It became the capital of Leyte in
and was chartered as a city on
. With direct flights from Manila and Cebu, a bridge across to Samar and van terminals serving every corner of Leyte, it works as the gateway for travel in Leyte and Samar.
On
October 20, 1944

, General MacArthur landed on the beach at Palo to the south, and three days later he proclaimed the restoration of the Philippine Commonwealth government at the Leyte Provincial Capitol in Tacloban; the city then served as the provisional capital where the Commonwealth government stayed until
February 27, 1945
. The city's patron is the Child Jesus, the Santo Niño. According to local tradition, in
the image was lost at sea while returning from restoration, and a cholera outbreak ended on the day it was recovered and brought home; that homecoming day,
June 30
, is still the city's biggest feast.
On
November 8, 2013
, the storm surge driven by super typhoon Haiyan (locally named Yolanda) rose

high in places, swamping coastal villages and the airport and leaving the city with its deepest wound. More than 6,000 people died across the Philippines, and Tacloban suffered the worst damage of all. The memorial park in Anibong, which keeps a cargo ship that the surge carried into the middle of the neighborhood, and the Holy Cross Memorial Cemetery in Basper, where many victims were buried together, keep that day in memory. The city has since bounced back quickly into a lively place with new malls and hotels.

Churches, museums, war sites and memorials are clustered in the city, so one or two days are enough to see them. Tacloban suits travelers interested in modern Philippine history and World War II, as well as those looking for an overnight base before or after heading to the caves of Samar or the islands off western Leyte. The
San Juanico Bridge
and the
Leyte Landing Memorial
, each
20–30 minutes
from the city by car, can be combined in half a day.
This white church stands on the corner where Real Street meets Zamora Street, and it is said to have begun as a parish founded by the Augustinians in
. Badly damaged by Haiyan, it was restored and raised to an archdiocesan shrine on
November 1, 2021

blocks.title: Santo Niño Shrine and Heritage Museum

children.text: This mansion was built by Imelda Marcos in
and is now a museum managed by a government agency (PCGG). On a guided tour of
30 minutes–1 hour
, you walk through 21 guest rooms each themed on a region of the Philippines, a banquet hall and the Santo Niño chapel, seeing the collections of a lavish era.
Built in
by the American Walter Scott Price, this mansion served as General MacArthur's quarters and headquarters for about three months in
. A hole that Japanese bombing punched in the roof above MacArthur's room has been preserved. It is privately owned, so visitors usually see the exterior and the statues from outside the wall.
This neoclassical building with two rows of Ionic columns was completed in
. From
October 23, 1944
, it served for a little over four months as the seat of the Philippine Commonwealth government. After an earthquake in
cracked the building and the provincial government moved to Palo, plans have been underway to turn it into a World War II museum.
This memorial park in Anibong keeps the bow of the cargo ship MV Eva Jocelyn exactly where the surge pushed it ashore, and it opened in
ahead of Haiyan's second anniversary. It still sits in the middle of a neighborhood where residents live, so visit quietly; during the November remembrance period, a Mass is held here.

blocks.title: Kanhuraw Hill and the Japanese Madonna

children.text: Along Magsaysay Boulevard below Kanhuraw Hill, where City Hall stands, is the Madonna of Peace, a Maria Kannon statue carved from stone from Mount Miyagi in Japan. With a face resembling Kannon, she holds a cross and a rosary, honoring the war dead and commemorating reconciliation between the Philippines and Japan.

Follow the large statues depicting the Passion of Christ up the hill, and at the top, beside the Resurrection scene, you take in the city's rooftops, the port, Cancabato Bay and the mountains across the water in one view. The path is steep, so climb with companions around
, when the sun eases off.
This seaside amphitheater faces Cancabato Bay and takes its name from the Balyuan rite, held since
. The rite reenacts the legend of an exchange of Santo Niño images with Basey in Samar. The mountains of Samar are visible across the water.
Start the day at the Santo Niño Church, then have a light breakfast at a bakery or café near the church.
Tour the Santo Niño Shrine and Heritage Museum with a guide.
See the exterior of the Price Mansion, then the former Leyte Provincial Capitol.
Have lunch of grilled fish and kinilaw at a downtown restaurant.
Stroll to City Hall and the Japanese Madonna at Kanhuraw Hill, then the seaside Balyuan Amphitheater.
Climb Calvary Hill to watch the sun sink over the city and Cancabato Bay.
Have dinner of grilled skewers at the barbecue stalls around Rizal Avenue.

items.title: Day 2
items.subtitle: Half-day side trip and a strait sunset

children.text: Take a jeepney or taxi
20–30 minutes
to the Leyte Landing Memorial in Palo to see the bronze statues and Red Beach.
Return to the city for lunch and buy moron and binagol at the market or a souvenir shop.
Visit the Yolanda Shipwreck Memorial in Anibong.
Watch the sunset and the night lighting from a San Juanico Bridge viewpoint, then head back to the city.

items.title: Remembering Haiyan
items.subtitle: Route for the November remembrance period

children.text: Visit the Holy Cross Memorial Cemetery in Basper, where many Haiyan victims were buried together; a memorial Mass is held there on
November 8
See the Yolanda memorial marker at the Tacloban Convention Center (Astrodome) facing Cancabato Bay. On the anniversary, flower offerings and candle-lighting ceremonies take place.
At the Yolanda Shipwreck Memorial in Anibong, see for yourself where the surge pushed a ship into the middle of the neighborhood.
Join an evening Mass at the Santo Niño Church, or walk the coastal road and look back on the rebuilt city.
These memorial sites are still visited by bereaved families, so look around quietly and follow instructions during ceremonies.
Flights from Manila to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport (TAC) take about
1 hour 15 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
, with daily service by Philippine Airlines (PAL Express), Cebu Pacific and AirAsia. The lowest one-way fares usually run around
and climb higher during holidays and festivals.
From Cebu, PAL Express and Cebgo fly in about
50 minutes–1 hour
. There are also routes from Davao (Cebu Pacific) and Iloilo (Cebgo), but they have few flights and change often.

items.title: From the airport to the city

children.text: The airport is in the San Jose district southeast of the city,
15–30 minutes
by taxi; airport dispatch taxis charge about
to downtown hotels.
For the cheapest option, walk out to the main road rather than boarding in front of the terminal and take a jeepney marked Downtown to avoid paying extra.
Fast craft such as OceanJet run from Cebu Pier 1 to Ormoc on western Leyte in about
2.5–3 hours
, at about
one way depending on seat class. In
, fuel surcharges were added and reduced repeatedly, so check the final fare in the operator's announcements.
Vans to Tacloban leave from the terminal near Ormoc port and take about
2.5–3 hours
for about
. The first van leaves at
, and the last one from Ormoc departs around

Long-distance buses to Tacloban, such as DLTB, leave from the Cubao and Pasay terminals in Manila, pass through the Bicol region, cross to Samar on the Matnog–Allen ferry and enter via the San Juanico Bridge. The trip takes about
22–28 hours
and costs about
, plus a possible fuel surcharge.
During periods of load limits on the San Juanico Bridge, the way large vehicles operate has changed before, so check how the bus crosses the bridge and its arrival time when you book.
The city is served by jeepneys and multicabs (about
per ride), tricycles and taxis. Jeepney fares rose on
September 28, 2026
, so check the fare chart inside the vehicle.
Tricycles have no meters, so agree on the fare before boarding. To cover several sights, a half-day charter is convenient.

Vans and buses to Ormoc, Basey, Palompon and other parts of Leyte and Samar leave from the new transport terminal (New Bus Terminal) in Abucay, northwest of downtown. Jeepneys toward Palo can be caught right on the city streets.
Tacloban has a tropical rainforest climate with no distinct dry season, and rain falls all year. The best time to visit is
March–June
, which brings relatively less rain and more clear days; the driest month is
April
and the hottest is
May
. From
November–February
, the northeast monsoon brings rain, making
December
the wettest month of the year, and from
July–December
the city often lies in the path of typhoons. Daytime highs hover around
year-round.
June
is the month of the Santo Niño fiesta. In
late June
, the Sangyaw Festival's parade of lights and the Balyuan rite are followed by the Pintados-Kasadyaan Festival, where dancers in tattoo body paint perform, and around the
June 30
feast day the Subiran Regatta of traditional sailboats is also held. However, Pintados-Kasadyaan was postponed in
, and in
some Sangyaw events were canceled due to fuel shortages, so the program changes every year. On
October 20
, the Leyte Landing anniversary is held in Palo, and on
November 8
, a Haiyan memorial Mass takes place.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
To visit the church and museum on foot, the downtown area around the Santo Niño Church and Real Street is convenient, with small hotels and pension houses at around
a night. Mid-range and chain hotels at about

a night are found near the big malls south and northwest of downtown and along the coastal road to the airport. Book early for the June fiesta and the year-end holidays. If you want a quiet stay by the sea, the resort-style hotels on the beach at Palo are another option.

The snacks to try in Tacloban are moron and binagol. Moron is a steamed rice cake of glutinous rice and rice flour mixed with coconut milk and chocolate (tablea) and wrapped in banana leaves; it is a snack of the Waray people of Eastern Visayas, and the Tacloban area in particular is regarded as its home. Binagol is a specialty of Leyte and Samar: a sweet paste of mashed giant taro mixed with coconut milk, condensed milk and egg yolks, packed into half a coconut shell, wrapped in banana leaves and tied with string. They are sold everywhere at markets, terminals and souvenir shops, making them good gifts to take home.

As befits a port city, there are many seafood restaurants serving grilled fish and squid, crab dishes and kinilaw, raw fish dressed in vinegar. In the evening, barbecue stalls around Rizal Avenue send up smoke, and you can enjoy a local-style dinner of grilled skewers, rice and cold drinks.
Chartering a tricycle or taxi for half a day lets you cover the church, museum, capitol and memorial park in one go.

The Santo Niño Shrine and Heritage Museum can be entered only on a guided tour, and its hours and fees change often. Visit in the morning or early afternoon, and ask on site about the rules for indoor photography.
In the church and the museum chapel, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and refrain from taking photos during Mass.
The path up Calvary Hill is steep and there are times when few people are around. Climb with companions around
, before sunset, and come down before dark.
The June fiesta's lineup and dates change every year. Check the Sangyaw parade and Balyuan rite schedules in announcements from the Tacloban City Tourism Office.
Vans to nearby towns run from early morning, but services thin out in the late afternoon and return trips can run out, so start day trips early.
The city has plenty of ATMs and malls, but tricycles, street stalls and markets take cash only, so carry plenty of small bills.
Typhoons pass frequently in
July–December

, and Tacloban is a coastal city that has suffered storm surge damage. When a typhoon signal is raised, avoid lodging in low-lying coastal areas, follow evacuation guidance from the city and the weather bureau (PAGASA), and book flights and ferries on changeable terms.
The San Juanico Bridge was placed under load limits in
May 2025
because of structural defects, and two-way traffic resumed under a 15-ton limit from
December 2025
. Restoring its original 33-ton capacity was targeted for completion in the third quarter of
, but no completion announcement has been confirmed, so check the latest notices from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) when planning bus or car trips to and from Samar.
In
, rising oil prices added fuel surcharges to fast craft and vans, so check fares and timetables just before you leave.
An anti-jaywalking ordinance is enforced in the city. Use crosswalks and obey traffic signals.
Watch out for pickpockets in crowded places such as markets and terminals, and do not keep your phone in a back pocket.
The interiors of the Price Mansion and the former capitol are not always open to the public. Do not climb the walls or enter without permission.
Dengue cases rise in the rainy season, so apply mosquito repellent and stay away from standing water.
